title: Hanaoka Seishū operates under general anaesthesia
summary: On 13 October 1804 the surgeon Hanaoka Seishū gave a 60-year-old woman, Kan Aiya, an oral herbal anaesthetic, tsūsensan, and removed a breast tumour while she was unconscious.
explanation:
Hanaoka Seishū (1760–1835) practised in Kii Province, combining Chinese-derived herbal medicine with surgical ideas reaching Japan through Dutch books. He spent years developing tsūsensan (also called mafutsusan), a drink based mainly on Datura and other plants, testing it on animals and, according to biographers, on members of his own family.

On 13 October 1804 he used it to anaesthetise Kan Aiya and excised her breast cancer. This is the earliest well-documented operation under general anaesthesia, more than four decades before ether was demonstrated in the United States. Hanaoka went on to perform many more operations with the drug and trained numerous students.

Because Japan's contacts with the outside world were tightly restricted at the time, his work was little known abroad and did not influence the later development of ether and chloroform anaesthesia in Europe and North America. The two lines developed independently.

title: A caesarean delivery observed in Bunyoro
summary: In 1879 a visiting medical student, Robert Felkin, watched practitioners in the kingdom of Bunyoro deliver a baby by caesarean section. Mother and child were alive when he left 11 days later.
explanation:
Robert Felkin was travelling with a missionary party in the Great Lakes region when, at a place he called Kahura, he witnessed a caesarean section carried out by a local surgeon and assistants. His account was presented to the Edinburgh Obstetrical Society in 1884.

According to Felkin, the patient, a young woman in her first pregnancy, was made half-intoxicated with banana wine, which was also used to wash the surgeon's hands and her abdomen. The surgeon opened the abdomen and uterus, delivered the baby, cleared the uterus of clots and the placenta, and closed the wound by pinning the edges together with iron spikes, covered with clean cloth. Felkin followed the mother and baby for 11 days and both did well.

Felkin concluded that the operation was well established. At the time, caesarean section in European hospitals still carried a very high maternal death rate, which makes the account notable, though it cannot be generalised from a single case.

title: Laveran sees the malaria parasite in a soldier's blood
summary: On 6 November 1880, at the military hospital in Constantine, the French army physician Alphonse Laveran saw moving parasites in the fresh blood of a soldier with malaria.
explanation:
Laveran had been posted to French military hospitals in Algeria, where malaria was common and often severe. Studying the dark pigment found in the blood of patients, he noticed unfamiliar bodies, and on 6 November 1880 at Constantine he watched one put out moving filaments, a sign that it was alive. He concluded that malaria was caused by a parasite, not a bacterium or a miasma.

He reported the finding to the French Academy of Medicine in November 1880. Many colleagues were sceptical, partly because others were searching for a 'malaria bacillus'; recognition came only gradually, by about 1889.

It was the first protozoan shown to cause an infectious disease, and it opened the way to the work on how malaria spreads.

title: Mosquitoes shown to carry malaria
summary: In 1897 Ronald Ross found malaria parasites developing in the stomach of an Anopheles mosquito that had fed on a patient. Over the next three years, Battista Grassi's team in Rome showed how human malaria is transmitted.
explanation:
Patrick Manson and Laveran had suggested that mosquitoes might spread malaria. Ronald Ross, an officer in the Indian Medical Service, spent more than two years dissecting mosquitoes before, on 20 August 1897 at Secunderabad, he found pigmented cysts in the stomach wall of an anopheline mosquito fed on a patient with malaria. He then worked out the full transmission cycle using a malaria parasite of birds.

In Italy, Giovanni Battista Grassi and colleagues showed that human malaria is transmitted specifically by Anopheles mosquitoes, confirming the cycle in humans by about 1900. Ross and Grassi quarrelled bitterly over priority; the 1902 Nobel Prize went to Ross alone.

Knowing the vector made it possible to attack malaria by controlling mosquitoes and their breeding sites, alongside treating the infection.

title: The Balmis expedition carries vaccine across two oceans
summary: From 1803 a Spanish royal expedition led by Francisco Xavier de Balmis carried smallpox vaccine to the Americas and Asia, keeping it alive by passing it arm to arm through a chain of orphaned children.
explanation:
Cowpox material lost its potency within days, so it could not survive a long voyage in a bottle. Balmis's solution was to take children who had never had smallpox and vaccinate them in sequence: as one child's pustule matured, fluid from it was used to vaccinate the next.

The expedition sailed from La Coruña on 30 November 1803 with 22 boys from an orphanage in Santiago de Compostela. In the Americas it divided. José Salvany led a branch through present-day Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia and Chile, a journey that lasted years, while Balmis took the vaccine to New Spain. There he recruited further children to carry it across the Pacific to the Philippines, and from there it reached Macao.

The expedition is often described as the first international, philanthropic vaccination campaign.

title: Semmelweis orders hand disinfection on a maternity ward
summary: In May 1847, at Vienna's General Hospital, Ignaz Semmelweis required doctors and medical students to wash their hands in chlorinated lime before examining women in labour. Deaths from puerperal fever fell sharply.
explanation:
Vienna's maternity hospital had two clinics, and women were admitted to them on alternate days. From 1840 to 1846, about 98 of every 1,000 mothers died in the first clinic, where doctors and medical students worked, against about 36 per 1,000 in the second, staffed by midwives. Almost all the deaths were from puerperal (childbed) fever.

Semmelweis concluded that students and doctors were carrying 'cadaverous particles' on their hands from the autopsy room to the delivery ward. From 15 May 1847 he required everyone to scrub with a chlorinated lime solution until the smell of the dissecting room was gone. Mortality in the first clinic fell to around the level of the midwives' clinic, and rose again after he left Vienna in 1850 and the practice lapsed.

His ideas were resisted, and he was slow to publish: students and colleagues reported his findings, and his own book appeared only in 1861. Germ theory, which explained why handwashing worked, came later.

title: John Snow traces a cholera outbreak to a water pump
summary: During the Soho cholera outbreak of 1854, John Snow gathered evidence that cases were linked to water from the Broad Street pump and persuaded local officials to remove its handle on 8 September.
explanation:
Many physicians at the time believed cholera spread through foul air, or miasma. John Snow, a London physician also known for his work on anaesthesia, argued that it was spread by something taken in by mouth, most likely in water.

When a severe outbreak struck Soho at the end of August 1854, killing more than 600 people, Snow examined the addresses of the dead and interviewed residents. Deaths clustered around the Broad Street pump, and telling exceptions fitted his theory: workers at a nearby brewery who drank beer escaped, while a woman living far away who had Broad Street water brought to her daily died. He presented his evidence to the parish board of guardians, and the pump handle was removed the next day, 8 September.

The outbreak was already declining by then, and the famous map of deaths was drawn afterwards to present the case rather than to discover it. Snow's broader argument that cholera is waterborne was not widely accepted in his lifetime.

title: Ether anaesthesia: a country practice and a public demonstration
summary: Crawford Long used ether during surgery in Jefferson, Georgia, in March 1842 but did not publicise it. On 16 October 1846 William Morton's public demonstration at Massachusetts General Hospital spread surgical anaesthesia around the world.
explanation:
The intoxicating effects of inhaled ether had been known for centuries. On 30 March 1842, Crawford Long, a physician in rural Georgia, etherised a patient, James Venable, to remove cysts from his neck, and went on to use ether in other operations. He did not report this promptly, so his work had no immediate influence.

On 16 October 1846, the Boston dentist William T. G. Morton administered sulphuric ether to Edward Gilbert Abbott in the surgical amphitheatre of Massachusetts General Hospital, now called the Ether Dome, while the surgeon John Collins Warren operated on a lesion under Abbott's jaw. Hospital records show the operation was a ligation of the lesion's blood supply rather than the tumour excision often described. The technique was quickly adopted around the world.

The demonstration was followed by twenty years of bitter dispute over credit between Morton, the chemist Charles Jackson and the dentist Horace Wells, none of whom had been first. Morton also tried to patent ether.

title: Lister treats a compound fracture with carbolic acid
summary: On 12 August 1865 at Glasgow Royal Infirmary, Joseph Lister dressed the open leg fracture of a boy, James Greenlees, with carbolic acid. The wound healed without infection, and Lister published the method in 1867.
explanation:
Compound fractures, where broken bone pierces the skin, frequently became infected and could lead to amputation or death. Lister, Regius Professor of Surgery at Glasgow, had read Louis Pasteur's work on microorganisms and reasoned that something entering the wound from outside caused the putrefaction.

When James Greenlees was brought in after being run over by a cart, Lister set the bone and dressed the wound with carbolic acid (phenol). The boy recovered fully. Lister treated further cases and in 1867 published a series of articles in The Lancet setting out what he called the antiseptic principle.

He later extended the approach to the surgical environment as a whole, using a carbolic spray during his years in Edinburgh.

title: Laennec invents the stethoscope
summary: In 1816 at the Necker Hospital in Paris, René Laennec rolled paper into a tube to listen to a patient's chest, then built a wooden stethoscope. His 1819 treatise linked the sounds he heard to findings at autopsy.
explanation:
Physicians sometimes listened to the chest by pressing an ear against it, which was awkward and often uninformative. According to the best-known account, Laennec was examining a young woman with suspected heart disease when he rolled a sheaf of paper into a tube and found that heart and breath sounds were much clearer through it. He soon replaced the paper with a wooden cylinder.

Laennec's real innovation was method. He systematically compared the sounds heard through the instrument with what he later found at post-mortem examination, building a vocabulary of signs such as rales and egophony. He set this out in De l'auscultation médiate (1819), which taught a generation of students from many countries.

Accounts differ on the date of the first use: some give February 1816, others 13 September 1816.

title: Antitoxin serum against diphtheria and tetanus
summary: In 1890, Emil von Behring and Kitasato Shibasaburō, working in Robert Koch's institute in Berlin, showed that serum from immunised animals could neutralise diphtheria and tetanus toxins and protect other animals. Serum therapy followed.
explanation:
Diphtheria killed large numbers of children by producing a toxin. Behring and Kitasato found that animals injected with the toxins of diphtheria or tetanus bacteria produced substances in their blood that neutralised them. Serum taken from such animals could protect untreated animals and even cure sick ones. They published their findings jointly in 1890.

Behring concluded that immunity could be transferred in the blood, an idea now called passive immunisation. Horse serum against diphtheria was soon tested in children, with an early report on 30 bacteriologically confirmed cases in 1893, and antitoxin was used in hospitals to reduce deaths during outbreaks by the mid-1890s. Similar work was under way in France at almost the same time.

The first Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, in 1901, went to Behring alone for serum therapy, although the foundational 1890 paper was co-authored with Kitasato.

title: Röntgen discovers X-rays
summary: On 8 November 1895 at the University of Würzburg, Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen noticed a fluorescent screen glowing near a shielded cathode-ray tube. He identified a new, penetrating radiation he called X-rays.
explanation:
Röntgen was experimenting with cathode-ray tubes when a fluorescent screen in his laboratory began to glow for no apparent reason. After weeks of work, often eating and sleeping in the laboratory, he showed that the tube emitted invisible rays able to pass through materials that were opaque to ordinary light. Because their nature was unknown, he called them X-rays.

He mailed his first announcement to colleagues on 1 January 1896, and the news spread around the world through the press. The discovery very soon made an impact on practical medicine, letting doctors see inside the body without surgery. Röntgen received the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901.

title: Koch identifies the cause of tuberculosis
summary: On 24 March 1882, at the Berlin Physiological Society, Robert Koch announced that he had found the bacterium that causes tuberculosis, then responsible for about one in seven deaths in Europe and the United States.
explanation:
Tuberculosis was widely thought to be hereditary or constitutional. Using new staining methods and culture media, Koch showed rod-shaped bacteria in tuberculous tissue from humans and animals, grew them in pure culture on blood serum, and reproduced the disease by inoculating animals with the cultures.

He presented his findings in a lecture on the aetiology of tuberculosis and published them three weeks later. In 1884 he set out the criteria, now called Koch's postulates, for linking a specific microbe to a specific disease, which became a foundation of bacteriology.

Identifying the cause did not immediately produce a cure; effective drugs arrived only in the 1940s. The anniversary of Koch's lecture has been observed as World TB Day since 1982.

title: Sertürner isolates morphine from opium
summary: Between 1803 and 1805 Friedrich Sertürner, a young pharmacist's assistant in Paderborn, isolated the sleep-inducing substance in opium. Named morphium after the god of dreams, it was the first alkaloid obtained from any plant.
explanation:
Sertürner trained at the court pharmacy in Paderborn. Just after finishing his apprenticeship he set out to find the substance responsible for opium's effects, and found that adding ammonia to a clarified opium extract separated an almost pure material. He first reported it in 1805 in a letter to a pharmaceutical journal, and soon described it as a weak base, which he called morphium.

The work drew little notice until 1817, when he published a full account of its isolation, crystallisation, chemistry and effects, tested on rats, dogs, himself and others. Small doses produced light-headed, happy feelings; larger ones caused drowsiness, exhaustion and confusion. He suggested it was the first of a new class of 'vegetable alkalis', and the word alkaloid was coined the following year.

A pure active ingredient could now be given in measured doses instead of crude opium. Commercial production began in 1827 at a pharmacy in Darmstadt that became the firm Merck.

title: Sims's fistula operations on enslaved women
summary: From 1845 to 1849, in a small hospital behind his house in Montgomery, Alabama, J. Marion Sims repeatedly operated without anaesthesia on enslaved women with vesicovaginal fistulas until he found a repair that worked. Three of the women are known by name: Anarcha, Betsey and Lucy.
explanation:
A vesicovaginal fistula, a hole between the bladder and vagina left by prolonged obstructed labour, caused constant leaking of urine and was generally considered incurable. Sims, a physician who treated enslaved people on plantations around Montgomery, devised a speculum that let him see the injury clearly and began experimental operations in late 1845.

About a dozen enslaved women, placed in his care by the people who enslaved them, were operated on over four years. Anarcha, aged 17, underwent 30 operations before her fistula closed in 1849. Sims never used anaesthesia in these operations, even after ether became available in 1846. The women also served as his nurses and surgical assistants once his colleagues stopped attending. No account by any of them survives.

Sims's success made his reputation, and he became one of the most celebrated surgeons of the nineteenth century, often called the father of modern gynaecology.

title: Blundell transfuses human blood
summary: From 1818 the London obstetrician James Blundell, determined to save women bleeding to death after childbirth, carried out the first documented transfusions of human blood into patients. His first patient died; in 1829 he published a case in which a woman with severe bleeding after childbirth recovered.
explanation:
Blundell, an obstetrician at Guy's Hospital, was, in his own words, appalled at his helplessness in the face of fatal haemorrhage during delivery. He experimented on dogs and, following the Edinburgh graduate John Leacock, who had argued that blood from another species was harmful, concluded that only human blood should be used.

In 1818 he transfused blood from several donors into a man dying of stomach cancer, who improved briefly but died two days later. Between 1818 and 1829 Blundell and his colleagues performed ten transfusions; at most four succeeded, and some patients were probably already dead. In 1829 The Lancet published a case in which a woman with severe bleeding after childbirth recovered after receiving eight ounces of blood, given gradually over three hours.

Blundell designed instruments for transfusion and promoted it widely, always crediting Leacock's earlier work. Without knowledge of blood groups, discovered almost a century later, transfusion remained risky and unpredictable.

title: Leukaemia recognised as a disease of the blood
summary: In 1845 John Hughes Bennett in Edinburgh, and six weeks later Rudolf Virchow in Germany, independently described patients whose blood was overwhelmed by white cells. Virchow called it 'white blood', and later leukämie.
explanation:
In March 1845 a slater named John Monteith died at the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh, where he had been under the care of Robert Christison, with a hugely enlarged spleen and liver. John Hughes Bennett examined the body and found the blood full of what he took to be pus cells, without any source of infection. He published the case later that year as one in which death came from 'suppuration of the blood'.

Six weeks after Bennett's report, Virchow, a young pathologist in Berlin, independently published a similar post-mortem case. Rather than calling it infection, he argued that the blood itself was abnormal, called the condition 'white blood' (weisses Blut) and two years later coined the name leukämie, from the Greek for white and blood.

The two men disputed priority for some years. Virchow eventually acknowledged Bennett's earlier publication.

title: Women begin to earn medical degrees in the United States
summary: In 1849 Elizabeth Blackwell became the first woman to receive an MD from an American medical school. In 1850 Quakers in Philadelphia founded the Female Medical College of Pennsylvania, the first medical school in the world for women authorised to award the MD.
explanation:
Women had long practised medicine as healers, nurses and midwives, but were barred from formal training as physicians. Elizabeth Blackwell, born in Bristol, England, applied to many medical schools before Geneva Medical College in western New York accepted her in 1847. On 23 January 1849 she received her degree in the town's Presbyterian church. She went on to support medical education for women in the United States and Britain.

In 1850, two years after the women's rights convention at Seneca Falls, a group of progressive physicians and laymen, most of them Quakers, chartered the Female Medical College of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia. It opened that year on Arch Street, and its first graduates, in 1851, included Ann Preston, who later became the first woman dean of an American medical school. The college, renamed the Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania in 1867, trained thousands of women physicians who practised around the world.

Opposition was fierce, and women students were openly harassed.

title: Virchow's Cellular Pathology
summary: In 1858 Rudolf Virchow published his Berlin lectures as Die Cellularpathologie, arguing that disease is a disturbance of the body's cells and that every cell arises from another cell. The idea displaced the ancient theory of imbalanced humours.
explanation:
Virchow trained in Berlin, held the first chair of pathological anatomy in Germany at Würzburg from 1849, and was recalled to Berlin in 1856 to lead its Pathological Institute. Early in 1858 he gave a series of 20 lectures there, published the same year as Cellular Pathology as Based upon Physiological and Pathological Histology.

Building on the recent theory that plants and animals are made of cells, Virchow argued that the cell is the basic unit of life and of disease: illnesses arise from changes in particular cells and tissues, and every cell comes from a pre-existing cell (omnis cellula e cellula). Disease, on this view, was to be found by examining tissues under the microscope, not by reasoning about imbalances of bodily fluids.

Virchow was also active in politics and public health; Berlin's modern sewer system owes much to him.

title: Pasteur's swan-neck flasks and the germ theory
summary: Between 1859 and 1862 Louis Pasteur showed in Paris that boiled broth stays sterile in a flask whose curved neck traps airborne dust, and spoils only when microbes from the air reach it. The work undermined spontaneous generation and supported the germ theory of disease.
explanation:
Many scientists still believed that microbes could arise spontaneously in decaying matter. Pasteur, whose work on fermentation had convinced him that it was caused by living micro-organisms, set out in 1859 to settle the question by experiment.

He boiled a nutrient liquid in a flask whose long neck he had drawn out into a downward S-curve, then let it cool. Air could still enter, but dust and germs settled in the bend of the neck, and the liquid stayed unaltered. Once the neck was broken, microbes soon grew in it. In 1862, after a public dispute with Félix Pouchet, a leading defender of spontaneous generation, he published his results.

Pasteur concluded that microbes are everywhere, in water, in air and on objects and skin, and that some of them cause disease. The idea underpinned Lister's antiseptic surgery and the later identification of specific disease-causing bacteria.

title: Pasteur's attenuated vaccines: chicken cholera and anthrax
summary: In 1879 Louis Pasteur's laboratory found that ageing cultures of the chicken cholera bacterium lost their virulence yet protected chickens. In May 1881 a public trial at Pouilly-le-Fort showed that an attenuated anthrax vaccine protected sheep, cattle and a goat.
explanation:
Inspired by Jenner, Pasteur hoped that vaccines could be found for all infectious diseases. In 1879 chickens inoculated with an old culture of the chicken cholera bacterium, left standing for weeks, became only mildly ill and then resisted fresh, virulent bacteria. Pasteur called this weakening 'attenuation' and attributed it to exposure to oxygen.

With Charles Chamberland and Émile Roux he then developed an anthrax vaccine. At a farm at Pouilly-le-Fort, near Paris, 24 sheep, a goat and six cows were vaccinated twice in May 1881 while a similar group was not. On 31 May all were injected with virulent anthrax. By 2 June the vaccinated animals were healthy, while the unvaccinated sheep and goat were dead and the unvaccinated cows ill. The trial, held before journalists and officials, made Pasteur's vaccine famous.

Chamberland's private notebooks, studied much later, show that the vaccine used at Pouilly-le-Fort had been weakened with potassium dichromate, a method close to that of Pasteur's rival Jean-Joseph Henri Toussaint, rather than by oxygen as Pasteur's public account implied.

title: Rabies vaccine given to Joseph Meister
summary: On 6 July 1885 in Paris, nine-year-old Joseph Meister, bitten 14 times by a rabid dog, began a course of injections of dried rabid spinal cord prepared in Louis Pasteur's laboratory. He never developed rabies, and the success led to the founding of the Institut Pasteur.
explanation:
Rabies was invariably fatal once symptoms appeared, but its long incubation offered time to act after a bite. Pasteur's team had weakened the rabies agent by air-drying the spinal cords of infected rabbits, and reported protecting dogs.

Meister's mother brought him from Alsace to Paris. Pasteur was not a physician, so Dr Jacques-Joseph Grancher gave the injections: 13 over about ten days, each made from progressively fresher, more virulent cord. Meister stayed well. In October a shepherd, Jean-Baptiste Jupille, was treated, and by March 1886 Pasteur reported results for 350 people. The flood of patients prompted the Academy of Sciences to call for a rabies vaccine centre, and the Institut Pasteur opened in 1888.

Pasteur's private notebooks, kept by his family until the 1970s, complicate the story. They record that he had treated two people before Meister, one of whom died, and that the preparation Meister received had been made by methods little tested in animals.

title: Snellen's eye chart
summary: In 1862 Herman Snellen of the Netherlands Hospital for Eye Patients in Utrecht published his optotypes: letters of graded sizes, each built on a 5 × 5 grid, for measuring sharpness of vision. Versions of his chart remain in use worldwide.
explanation:
Earlier tests, such as Eduard Jäger's reading-type cards, measured how well people could read ordinary print of various sizes. Snellen, assistant and then first physician at the eye hospital founded in Utrecht by Franciscus Donders, chose not to use existing typefaces. He designed special letters, which he called optotypes, each drawn within a square divided into 5 × 5 parts, so that the detail of each letter had a defined size.

Visual acuity could then be expressed as a fraction: the distance at which the person reads a line, over the distance at which a normal eye can just read it. He published the charts in 1862.

Snellen later became professor of ophthalmology at Utrecht in 1877 and director of the eye hospital in 1884.

title: Recording the heart's electrical activity
summary: In May 1887 Augustus Waller recorded the first electrocardiogram from a human heart at St Mary's Hospital, London. Willem Einthoven, who saw Waller's demonstrations, built a far more sensitive string galvanometer at Leiden and by 1903 was recording clear, clinically useful ECGs.
explanation:
Waller used a capillary electrometer, in which a mercury column moves slightly with electric current, and photographed the shadow of the moving meniscus on a travelling plate. His 1887 tracings from the intact human heart showed only two distorted deflections, and he doubted that the method would ever be much use in hospitals.

Einthoven, professor of physiology at Leiden, first corrected the distortions of the capillary electrometer mathematically and named the deflections P, Q, R, S and T. He then developed a string galvanometer, a fine silver-coated quartz thread stretched between the poles of a strong magnet, which he described in 1901 and used to publish detailed ECGs in 1903.

It made the electrocardiogram a practical tool for detecting heart disease. Einthoven received the 1924 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

title: Ellis Shipp's school of obstetrics and nursing, Utah
summary: After graduating from the Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania in March 1878, Ellis Reynolds Shipp returned to Salt Lake City and opened a school of obstetrics and nursing. Over five decades it trained about 500 women as midwives and nurses across Utah.
explanation:
Leaders of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, concerned about deaths of mothers and infants in Utah Territory, encouraged women to train as physicians in the East. Shipp took the place of a homesick sister wife at the Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania and graduated on 14 March 1878.

Back in Salt Lake City she set up a practice in obstetrics and women's diseases and, realising that a few women doctors could not meet the need, opened a school to train midwives and nurses, advertised with free scholarships. Its graduates became licensed midwives in communities throughout the territory. Shipp herself is said to have delivered more than 5,000 babies, and she helped found the Deseret Hospital.
